chunks: Al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb narrated this hadith in Kitāb al-Mashīkhah with another wording, from ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, who said:

I performed ghusl on Friday in al-Madīnah, put on my clothes, and applied perfume. Then a slave-girl passed by me, and I pressed my thigh against her, so I emitted madhy and she had emission. This caused me distress, so I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about that, and he said: “There is no wudu (ablution) upon you, and there is no ghusl upon her.”

So it is possible that the hearer erred in what he heard, and that he had actually said: “she emitted madhy,” but it occurred to him as “she emitted maniyy,” so he narrated it according to what he presumed. And it is also possible that he عليه السلام only answered him according to what appeared to him from his condition at that moment, and knew that he believed that she had emitted maniyy while that was not so; thus he عليه السلام answered him according to what the ruling required, not according to his belief.

key_terms.أَمْنَتْ: she emitted maniyy, as understood in the report
key_terms.الْجُمُعَةِ: Friday, the day on which the event occurred
key_terms.الْحُكْمُ: the legal ruling applicable to the case
key_terms.غُسْلٌ: ghusl (ritual bath), the major ritual purification

ai.seo_question: Does emission after intimate contact without intercourse require wudu (ablution) or ghusl in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This report discusses a legal ruling related to ritual purity after intimate contact without intercourse, focusing on whether wudu (ablution) or ghusl becomes obligatory. The closing discussion considers how the wording of the report may be understood and reconciled in light of the legal ruling.
